questions.prompt: In C++23, what does this program print?
questions.explanation: Since C++20, `std::erase_if` on a `vector` performs the erase-remove idiom for you and returns the number of elements it removed. Three even numbers go, so `n` is 3 and the size drops from 6 to 3. The tempting `3 6` imagines `std::remove_if` alone, which shuffles elements but leaves the size unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which of the three calls is ill-formed?
questions.explanation: `emplace_back` forwards its arguments to a constructor call, so an explicit constructor is fine. `push_back(P(2))` passes an actual `P`. `push_back(3)` needs an implicit conversion from `int` to `P` to bind the `value_type` parameter, and an explicit constructor forbids that, so only (3) is rejected.

questions.prompt: What is the behavior of this program?
options: Well-formed; element 0 is written but `size()` stays 0
questions.explanation: `reserve` only allocates capacity; it creates no elements and leaves `size()` at 0. `operator[]` does no bounds check, and indexing at or past `size()` is undefined behavior, even though the storage exists. `at` would throw `std::out_of_range`, which is the tempting but wrong description of `operator[]`.

options: Undefined behavior: the reference was invalidated
questions.explanation: Insertion at either end of a `deque` invalidates iterators but never references or pointers to existing elements. The original element 2 sits at index 1001 after 1000 `push_front` calls, and `r` still names it, so the write is well-defined and the program prints 99. The same program using an iterator instead of `r` would be undefined behavior, which is what makes the first option tempting.

options: Undefined behavior: `it` is invalidated by the splice
questions.explanation: `splice` relinks nodes without copying or destroying anything. Iterators to the moved element stay valid, keep referring to the same element, and now behave as iterators into `b`. The element 1 is the new last element of `b`, so `std::next(it)` equals `b.end()`, and `a` is left with two elements. The third option imagines `it` still belonging to `a`.

questions.prompt: With libstdc++ or libc++, what does this program print after `grow`? (The standard only demands the strong exception guarantee; this is what both implementations do for a copyable type.)
options: One `move` line for each old element
One `copy` line for each old element
Nothing; growth never touches the old elements
One `move` line, then the old elements are copied
questions.explanation: To keep the strong guarantee, `vector` relocates with `std::move_if_noexcept`: elements are moved only if the move constructor is `noexcept` or the type cannot be copied. Here the move constructor may throw and a copy constructor exists, so every old element is copied, and the originals stay intact if a copy throws. Marking the move constructor `noexcept` would flip the output to `move`.

questions.prompt: Is this program well-formed in C++23?
questions.explanation: `forward_list` is specified as a container that omits `size()`, so that it can keep the same space overhead as a hand-written singly linked list. Use `std::distance(f.begin(), f.end())` and accept the linear cost. `list`, by contrast, has a constant-time `size()` since C++11.

questions.prompt: In C++23, what does this program print?
questions.explanation: C++23 added range-aware members. `insert_range` returns an iterator to the first inserted element (the 8), and `append_range` returns `void`. The vector goes from 2 to 4 to 6 elements. Dereferencing `it` before the append matters, because a reallocation in `append_range` would invalidate it.
